specStatements.text: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Rusting is an example of corrosion. Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.
Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier, such as greasing, painting or electroplating. Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.
Some coatings are reactive and contain a more reactive metal to provide sacrificial protection, eg zinc is used to galvanise iron.
Students should be able to:
describe experiments and interpret results to show that both air and water are necessary for rusting
explain sacrificial protection in terms of relative reactivity.
Most metals in everyday use are alloys.
Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc. The proportion of gold in the alloy is measured in carats. 24 carat being 100% (pure gold), and 18 carat being 75% gold.

Steels are alloys of iron that contain specific amounts of carbon and other metals. High carbon steel is strong but brittle. Low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped. Steels containing chromium and nickel (stainless steels) are hard and resistant to corrosion.
Aluminium alloys are low density.
Students should be able to:
recall a use of each of the alloys specified
interpret and evaluate the composition and uses of alloys other than those specified given appropriate information.

Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone. Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.
Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating in a furnace.

The properties of polymers depend on what monomers they are made from and the conditions under which they are made. For example, low density (LD) and high density (HD) poly(ethene) are produced from ethene.
Thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated. Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated.
Students should be able to:
explain how low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene
explain the difference between thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers in terms of their structures.
Most composites are made of two materials, a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material, which is called the reinforcement.
Students should be able to recall some examples of composites.
Students should be able to, given appropriate information:
compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals
explain how the properties of materials are related to their uses and select appropriate materials.

scopeNotes.statement: Corrosion can be prevented by applying a coating that acts as a barrier, such as greasing, painting or electroplating.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the three barrier methods the specification names are taught - greasing, painting and electroplating - together with the sacrificial coatings of the next statement. Electroplating is treated only as a way of laying down a barrier layer of another metal; the electrode reactions, half equations and cell arrangements of electrolysis belong to 4.3 and are not brought in here. No equation for rusting is stated, because the specification states none in this section.

scopeNotes.statement: The proportion of gold in the alloy is measured in carats. 24 carat being 100% (pure gold), and 18 carat being 75% gold.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Carats are treated exactly as the specification defines them - a measure of the proportion of gold, with the two anchor values 24 carat = 100% and 18 carat = 75%. Any other carat value is handled only as arithmetic on that same scale (carats divided by 24), and students are never asked to recall further carat values, hallmarking conventions or the proportions of silver, copper and zinc in a particular piece of jewellery, none of which the specification gives.

scopeNotes.statement: interpret and evaluate the composition and uses of alloys other than those specified given appropriate information.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Alloys beyond bronze, brass, gold alloys, the steels and aluminium alloys appear only inside questions that supply the composition and property data needed, in line with 'given appropriate information'. No composition of an unspecified alloy is ever presented as something to memorise.

scopeNotes.statement: explain how low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The explanation is kept to what the specification supports: the same monomer, ethene, gives two different materials because different catalysts and different reaction conditions are used, and the specification states that the properties of polymers depend on the monomers and on the conditions under which they are made. Named industrial catalysts and specific temperatures and pressures are not stated by the specification and are not taught or examined here.

scopeNotes.statement: compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every quantitative comparison question supplies the data in the stem, as 'given appropriate information' requires. No student is expected to recall a density, a melting point or a strength value for any material in this section; the skill assessed is reading and using supplied figures to choose a material.

concepts.definition: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. It is a chemical change, not simply wear, and it is not limited to metals.
The corrosion of iron. Rusting is an example of corrosion, and both air and water are necessary for iron to rust: remove either one and no rust forms.
A layer applied to a metal that keeps air and water away from the metal surface, so corrosion cannot happen. Greasing, painting and electroplating are the examples the specification gives.
Covering the surface of one metal with a thin layer of another metal. In this topic it matters only as a way of putting a barrier coating onto a metal to prevent corrosion.

Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion. The layer forms on the surface, stays firmly attached and stops air and water reaching the aluminium underneath, so the metal behaves as though it were unreactive.

Protecting a metal by putting it in contact with a more reactive metal. The more reactive metal corrodes in preference to the metal being protected, and it goes on doing so even where the coating is scratched or broken.
Coating iron with zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so a galvanised coating acts both as a barrier and as sacrificial protection.
Water that has been boiled to drive out dissolved air and then covered with a layer of oil to stop air dissolving back in. It is the control used to test whether air is necessary for rusting.
A substance that absorbs water vapour. Sealed in a tube with an iron nail, it leaves the nail surrounded by dry air, which is the control used to test whether water is necessary for rusting.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Most metals in everyday use are alloys rather than pure metals.
An alloy of copper and tin. It is used for statues, bells, medals and ornaments.
An alloy of copper and zinc. It is used for musical instruments such as trumpets and horns, and for taps, door fittings and other fixtures.
Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc, because pure gold is too soft to wear well. Jewellery is the use to recall for this alloy.
The measure of the proportion of gold in a gold alloy, on a scale of 24. 24 carat is 100% gold (pure gold) and 18 carat is 75% gold.
An alloy of iron that contains specific amounts of carbon and other metals. Changing how much carbon and which other metals are present changes the properties of the steel.
Steel with a higher proportion of carbon. It is strong but brittle, which suits it to cutting tools and blades.
Steel with a lower proportion of carbon. It is softer and more easily shaped, which suits it to sheet products such as car body panels.
Steel containing chromium and nickel. Stainless steels are hard and resistant to corrosion, which suits them to cutlery, sinks and chemical plant.
An alloy of aluminium. Aluminium alloys are low density, which is why they are chosen for aircraft bodies and bicycle frames where weight matters.
The glass used for most everyday purposes, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide. It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass, which is why it is chosen where glass must be heated.
A material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace. The clay is fired, not melted.
The small molecule that polymer chains are built from. The properties of a polymer depend on what monomers it is made from and on the conditions under which it is made.
Low density poly(ethene), produced from the monomer ethene under one set of catalyst and reaction conditions. It is the less dense and more flexible of the two forms.
High density poly(ethene), produced from the same monomer, ethene, but using a different catalyst and different reaction conditions. It is the denser and stiffer of the two forms.
A polymer that melts when it is heated. Its structure is separate polymer chains, tangled together but not joined to each other, so heating lets the chains move apart.
A polymer that does not melt when it is heated. Its chains are joined to each other by cross-links, so the chains cannot move apart and the material keeps its shape when hot.
A material made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material.
The continuous material in a composite that surrounds the reinforcement and binds it together, such as the cement in concrete or the resin in fibreglass.
The fibres or fragments held within the matrix of a composite, such as the gravel in concrete or the glass fibres in fibreglass.
A composite of glass fibres as the reinforcement held in a matrix of polymer resin. It is an example to recall, along with concrete and carbon fibre.
A composite in which fragments of gravel and sand are the reinforcement, bound together by a matrix of cement. Wood is an example of a natural composite.

A measurable property such as density, strength, hardness or melting point. Given data for glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals, these values are compared to explain uses and to select an appropriate material.

misconceptions.question: Iron left in a puddle rusts. Does that mean water on its own causes rusting?
misconceptions.correct: Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust; water alone will not do it.
misconceptions.misconception: Water is what makes iron rust, so anything wet will rust and the air has nothing to do with it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every rusty object a student has seen has been wet at some point, and air is invisible and always present, so it never registers as a variable. Water is the change they can see.
misconceptions.correction: A nail in water that has been boiled to remove dissolved air and sealed under a layer of oil does not rust, even though it is completely wet. The only difference from the tube that does rust is the air, so air must be necessary too.

misconceptions.question: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, so why do aluminium window frames not corrode away?
misconceptions.correct: Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.
misconceptions.misconception: Aluminium must be an unreactive metal, because it never seems to corrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge reactivity by what they observe. Aluminium objects stay bright for years, which contradicts the reactivity series they have been taught, and the simplest way to resolve the clash is to decide aluminium is unreactive.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium is reactive; it reacts quickly with oxygen. The oxide it forms stays firmly attached as a thin coating that seals the surface, so air and water cannot reach the metal below and the corrosion stops there.

misconceptions.question: How does painting a steel gate stop it rusting?
misconceptions.correct: The paint acts as a barrier, keeping air and water away from the metal surface.
misconceptions.misconception: Painting or greasing changes the metal so it is less reactive and no longer wants to rust.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the coating stops the rusting and reach for a chemical explanation, treating the coating as something that alters the metal rather than something that simply gets in the way.
misconceptions.correction: The iron underneath is unchanged and still just as reactive. The coating only separates it from air and water. That is why a chip in the paint lets rust start immediately at that spot.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is used to galvanise iron. Is the zinc chosen because it is less reactive than iron?
misconceptions.correct: Zinc is chosen because it is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in preference to the iron.
misconceptions.misconception: The protecting metal must be the less reactive one, otherwise it would corrode away and be useless.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everywhere else in the course, unreactive metals are the ones that survive, and students transfer that rule. The idea of deliberately choosing a metal that will be destroyed feels like the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Sacrificial protection works precisely because the coating is more reactive. The zinc is attacked instead of the iron, and the iron survives while any zinc remains, which is the point of the sacrifice.

misconceptions.question: A galvanised bucket gets a deep scratch through the zinc. Will the iron now rust there?
misconceptions.correct: No. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc corrodes instead, even where the iron is exposed.
misconceptions.misconception: Galvanising is just a zinc layer, so as soon as it is scratched the iron underneath is exposed and rusts like any other bare iron.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have just learnt that barrier coatings fail when scratched, and they apply that rule to every coating without noticing that a reactive coating protects by a second, different mechanism.
misconceptions.correction: Galvanising does two jobs. It is a barrier, and it is sacrificial protection. Because zinc is the more reactive metal, it continues to corrode in preference to the iron even when the iron is exposed at a scratch.

misconceptions.question: Copper roofs turn green over time. Is that copper rusting?
misconceptions.correct: It is corrosion, but not rusting. Rusting is the name for the corrosion of iron.
misconceptions.misconception: Rusting is what all metals do when they corrode, so any corroded metal has rusted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rust is the only corrosion product most students can name, so the word gets used for every case of a metal being eaten away by its surroundings.
misconceptions.correction: Corrosion is the general term for the destruction of materials by chemical reaction with substances in the environment. Rusting is one example of corrosion, and it is specific to iron.

misconceptions.question: Is corrosion something that only happens to metals?
misconceptions.correct: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment, and materials other than metals can be attacked in this way.
misconceptions.misconception: Corrosion means metal being eaten away, so only metals can corrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every worked example a student meets is a metal, and the definition is usually first met alongside rusting, so the general word gets narrowed to the one case.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition as it stands: it says materials, not metals. Stonework attacked by acidic rainwater is destroyed by a chemical reaction with a substance in its environment, which fits the definition exactly.

misconceptions.question: In the rusting experiment, the nail in dry air with calcium chloride does not rust. What has that tube proved?
misconceptions.correct: It shows that water is necessary, because air was present and rusting still did not occur.
misconceptions.misconception: The tube with no rusting proves that whatever was in it stops rusting - the calcium chloride, or the oil, must be a rust preventer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read each tube as a separate result instead of as one variable removed from a fair test, and they focus on the unfamiliar chemical rather than on which condition it has taken away.
misconceptions.correction: Each tube removes one thing. The calcium chloride removes water while leaving air; no rust means water is necessary. The boiled water under oil removes air while leaving water; no rust means air is necessary. The chemicals are the method, not the explanation.

misconceptions.question: Brass is harder than copper and harder than zinc. Does that make brass a compound of copper and zinc?
misconceptions.correct: Brass is an alloy, which is a mixture of copper and zinc, not a compound.
misconceptions.misconception: The properties of an alloy are different from the metals it is made from, so a new substance must have been formed, which means it is a compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught that compounds have properties unlike their elements, and they run that rule backwards: different properties therefore compound. Alloys are also made by melting things together, which looks like a reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The elements in an alloy are not chemically joined in fixed proportions; they are mixed. The property change comes from atoms of different sizes disrupting the regular layers, not from a new compound being formed.

misconceptions.question: Which is copper and tin, bronze or brass?
misconceptions.correct: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
misconceptions.misconception: Brass is the one with tin in it, and bronze is copper with zinc.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two alloys are learnt together, share copper, and both have short similar names, so the second element is the only thing to remember and it is easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Pair the initials: bronze and tin both appear in bell metal for statues and bells; brass and zinc go together in trumpets and taps. Bronze - tin; brass - zinc.

misconceptions.question: A ring is sold as 18 carat. Is the carat number telling you how heavy the ring is?
misconceptions.correct: For gold alloys the carat measures the proportion of gold in the alloy, on a scale where 24 carat is 100% gold.
misconceptions.misconception: Carats measure how much gold there is by mass, so a bigger, heavier ring has more carats.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carat is also used as a unit of mass for gemstones, and advertising uses the word loosely, so students attach it to size or weight rather than to composition.
misconceptions.correction: Carats here are a proportion out of 24. An 18 carat ring is 75% gold whether it weighs 2 g or 20 g; only the fraction of gold is being described.

misconceptions.question: What percentage of an 18 carat gold ring is gold?
misconceptions.correct: 75%, because the carat scale runs to 24 and 18 out of 24 is 75%.
misconceptions.misconception: 18 carat gold must be 18% gold, so most of the ring is other metals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentages are the only proportional scale most students use daily, so the number is read as one directly, without noticing that the scale tops out at 24 rather than 100.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor on the top of the scale: 24 carat is 100% gold. Divide by 24 and multiply by 100 for any other value, so 18 carat gives 18 divided by 24, which is 75%.

misconceptions.question: High carbon steel is stronger than low carbon steel. Does that make it the better choice for a car body panel?
misconceptions.correct: No. High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped, which is what a pressed panel needs.
misconceptions.misconception: Strength is what matters in engineering, so the strongest steel is always the right one to pick.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Strong is an unambiguously positive word, while brittle and soft sound like faults. Students rank materials on a single scale of good to bad instead of matching a property to a job.
misconceptions.correction: Match the property to the demand. A panel must be pressed into shape without cracking, so it needs a steel that is easily shaped. Strength that comes with brittleness would make the panel crack in the press and shatter on impact.

misconceptions.question: What makes stainless steel resistant to corrosion?
misconceptions.correct: It is a steel that contains chromium and nickel; these are alloyed all the way through the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: Stainless steel is ordinary steel with a shiny chromium coating on the outside that stops it rusting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have just learnt about electroplating as a barrier coating, and stainless steel looks exactly like chrome plating, so the two are merged.
misconceptions.correction: The chromium and nickel are part of the alloy, not a layer on it. That is why a stainless steel knife that has been ground or scratched still does not rust, unlike a plated object that has lost its coating.

misconceptions.question: Is steel a pure metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. Steels are alloys of iron that contain specific amounts of carbon and other metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Steel is what you get when you purify iron properly, so steel is basically pure iron with a different name.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Steel is presented as the better, more useful version of iron, and better is read as purer. Students also see steel treated as a single named material, which makes it sound like an element.
misconceptions.correction: Steel is deliberately impure: carbon is added in controlled amounts, and other metals such as chromium and nickel are added to change the properties. Different steels have different compositions, which is why they have different properties.

misconceptions.question: Why are aluminium alloys used to build aircraft?
misconceptions.correct: Aluminium alloys are low density, so the aircraft is much lighter than one built from steel.
misconceptions.misconception: Aluminium must be the strongest metal there is, otherwise it would not be trusted to build an aeroplane.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume the most demanding application must use the best material, and best defaults to strongest. The property that actually decides the choice, density, is not one they think of as a selling point.
misconceptions.correction: Steel is stronger than an aluminium alloy. Aluminium alloys are chosen because of their low density: less mass to lift means less fuel, and enough strength for the job is achieved by alloying and by the design.

misconceptions.question: What is borosilicate glass made from?
misconceptions.correct: Sand and boron trioxide. Soda-lime glass is the one made from sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
misconceptions.misconception: Borosilicate glass is the ordinary mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone with some boron added to make it heatproof.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Soda-lime glass is met first and becomes the default recipe, so the second glass is treated as a modification of it rather than as a different mixture.
misconceptions.correction: Learn them as two separate recipes. Soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate, limestone. Borosilicate glass: sand and boron trioxide, and it melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

misconceptions.question: Are clay ceramics made by melting the clay?
misconceptions.correct: No. Clay ceramics are made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.
misconceptions.misconception: Bricks and pottery must be melted and poured into moulds, the way glass and metals are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Glass and metal shaping are met alongside ceramics and both involve melting, so students generalise. The word furnace also suggests melting rather than firing.
misconceptions.correction: The shaping happens first, while the clay is wet and soft. The heating in the furnace then hardens the shape that has already been made. The clay is fired, not melted and poured.

misconceptions.question: LD and HD poly(ethene) have different properties. Are they made from different monomers?
misconceptions.correct: No. Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene, using different catalysts and different reaction conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Different polymers must come from different monomers, so high density poly(ethene) is made from some denser starting molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a polymer is named after its monomer and that properties depend on the monomer, so they conclude that the monomer is the only thing that can be different.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says properties depend on the monomers and on the conditions under which the polymer is made. Here the monomer is the same and the conditions differ: a different catalyst and different reaction conditions give chains that pack differently, and so a different density.

misconceptions.question: Why does a thermosetting polymer not melt when it is heated?
misconceptions.correct: Its polymer chains are joined to each other by cross-links, so the chains cannot separate and move apart.
misconceptions.misconception: Thermosetting polymers have much longer and heavier chains than thermosoftening ones, and long chains need more heat to melt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that longer chains raise the melting point of simple molecules, then stretch that idea to explain a material that does not melt at all rather than one that melts at a higher temperature.
misconceptions.correction: The difference is between chains, not along them. In a thermosoftening polymer separate chains slide apart on heating. In a thermosetting polymer covalent cross-links hold the chains to one another, so no amount of heating lets them flow.

misconceptions.question: When a thermosoftening polymer melts, what is being broken?
misconceptions.correct: The weak forces between the separate polymer chains, which lets the chains move past one another. The covalent bonds within the chains stay intact.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting a polymer breaks the covalent bonds in the chains, which is why the plastic goes runny.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Melting is described as breaking bonds in loose speech, and students do not distinguish the strong bonds along a chain from the weak forces holding neighbouring chains together.
misconceptions.correction: If the covalent bonds broke, the polymer would be destroyed and could not be remoulded. Thermosoftening plastics can be melted and reshaped repeatedly, which shows only the forces between chains have been overcome.

misconceptions.question: Is an alloy such as brass a composite material?
misconceptions.correct: No. A composite is a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a reinforcement, which are still separate materials within it.
misconceptions.misconception: A composite is anything made by mixing two materials together, so alloys and even solutions count as composites.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of composite is simply made of parts, and students meet alloys and composites in the same topic as two kinds of mixed material.
misconceptions.correction: Look for the two distinct parts still present and doing different jobs: a continuous matrix, and fibres or fragments held inside it. In brass the zinc atoms are mixed among the copper atoms; there is no matrix and no reinforcement.

misconceptions.question: In fibreglass, which part is the matrix and which is the reinforcement?
misconceptions.correct: The resin is the matrix that surrounds and binds; the glass fibres are the reinforcement.
misconceptions.misconception: The fibres are the matrix, because they run right through the material and hold it all together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word matrix suggests a framework or network, and the fibres are the visible framework, so the two labels are swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The matrix is the continuous material that surrounds the other one. Ask which part is doing the surrounding: the resin flows around the fibres, so the resin is the matrix and the fibres are the reinforcement.

misconceptions.question: Is any material containing fibres a composite?
misconceptions.correct: No. A composite needs a matrix or binder surrounding and binding the fibres or fragments of reinforcement.
misconceptions.misconception: Composites are the materials with fibres in them, so cloth, rope and wool count and concrete does not.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fibreglass and carbon fibre are the examples students remember, and both have fibre in the name, so fibre becomes the test instead of the two-part structure.
misconceptions.correction: Check for both parts. Woven cloth is fibres alone with nothing binding them. Concrete has fragments of gravel bound by a matrix of cement, so concrete is a composite and cloth is not.

misconceptions.question: Given data for several materials, is the strongest one always the right choice?
misconceptions.correct: No. The property that matters depends on the job, so density, cost, brittleness and resistance to corrosion may decide it instead.
misconceptions.misconception: When you compare materials you pick the strongest, because strength is the property that shows how good a material is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a single ranking of materials from best to worst, and strength is the property they can most easily interpret, so it dominates their reading of a data table.
misconceptions.correction: Start from what the object has to do, then read only the columns that matter to it. A frame that must be light and stay outdoors is decided by density and corrosion resistance, even if a stronger material appears in the table.

misconceptions.question: Does the oxide layer on aluminium flake off like rust does on iron?
misconceptions.correct: No. The aluminium oxide coating stays attached to the surface and protects the metal from further corrosion.
misconceptions.misconception: All oxide layers crumble away and expose fresh metal, so aluminium must need repainting like iron does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rust is the students' model of what a metal oxide does, and rust does flake away. They generalise the behaviour of one oxide to all of them.
misconceptions.correction: Rust flakes off, so fresh iron is exposed and corrosion continues into the metal. Aluminium oxide adheres firmly and seals the surface, so the reaction stops. The difference in behaviour of the oxide is the whole reason aluminium survives outdoors.

misconceptions.question: Steel food cans are coated with tin. Does the tin protect the steel sacrificially?
misconceptions.correct: No. Tin is less reactive than iron, so it protects only as a barrier; sacrificial protection needs a more reactive metal.
misconceptions.misconception: Any metal coating gives sacrificial protection, because the coating is always the part that gets attacked first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Zinc on iron is the only example students meet, and they generalise from it without checking the relative reactivity that makes the example work.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the two metals in the reactivity series first. Zinc above iron means zinc corrodes instead of the iron, so the protection survives a scratch. Tin below iron means a scratched tin coating leaves the exposed iron to corrode.

misconceptions.question: Does iron need salt water to rust?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both air and water are necessary for iron to rust; salt is not one of the necessary conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: Rusting is caused by salt, so iron kept away from salty water or salted roads will not rust.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that salt water and gritted roads make cars rust badly, and they turn a factor that speeds rusting up into a factor that is required for it.
misconceptions.correction: A nail in ordinary tap water with air present rusts perfectly well, which shows salt is not necessary. Salt increases the rate of rusting; the two necessary conditions remain air and water.

misconceptions.question: A data table shows one alloy is denser than another. Does that mean it is stronger?
misconceptions.correct: No. Density and strength are separate properties and must each be read from the data provided.
misconceptions.misconception: A denser material has more packed into it, so it must also be the stronger and harder one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heavy objects feel solid and substantial, and students merge the ideas of heavy, strong and hard into one vague notion of toughness rather than treating them as distinct measurable properties.
misconceptions.correction: Treat each column separately. A dense alloy can be soft, and a low density alloy can be strong enough for the job. Only the strength figures given can answer a question about strength.

misconceptions.question: Will a thermosetting polymer melt if it is heated hot enough?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated; they char or burn instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything melts eventually, so a thermosetting polymer just has a very high melting point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have met melting point as a property that every substance has, so a material that never melts does not fit their model and gets recast as one that is simply hard to melt.
misconceptions.correction: The cross-links between the chains are covalent and hold the whole structure together, so there is no temperature at which the chains can slide apart and flow. Heat it strongly and it chars rather than melting.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by corrosion?

options.text: Damage that only metals suffer, caused by the air around them
options.rationale: Every example a student meets is a metal, so the general word gets narrowed to metals only.

options.text: Destruction of a material by chemical reactions with substances around it
options.rationale: This is the definition: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.

options.text: The rusting of any metal that is left standing in air and water
options.rationale: Rust is the only corrosion product students can name, so rusting is used as a synonym for corrosion.

options.text: Gradual wearing away of a surface by scratching, rubbing and use
options.rationale: Corrosion is confused with mechanical wear, because both leave a surface eaten away.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?

options.text: Water alone; the air makes no difference
options.rationale: Wetness is the visible change students associate with rust, and air is never noticed as a variable.

options.text: Salt water, or water that contains an acid
options.rationale: Salted roads and sea air are known to cause bad rusting, so salt is promoted to a requirement.

options.text: Both air and water in contact with the iron
options.rationale: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

options.text: Air alone, provided the iron is left warm
options.rationale: Mirrors the water-only error: one condition is kept and the other is dropped.

mcqs.stem: Three iron nails are sealed in tubes. Tube 1: nail in tap water, open to air. Tube 2: nail in water that has been boiled, covered by a layer of oil. Tube 3: nail in dry air over anhydrous calcium chloride. Only the nail in tube 1 rusts. What does the result for tube 2 show?

options.text: Water is not necessary, since this nail was wet and did not rust
options.rationale: Students read one tube in isolation instead of identifying the single variable that has been removed.

options.text: Air is necessary, since the wet nail did not rust without it
options.rationale: Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil stops it returning, so tube 2 has water but no air, and no rust forms.

options.text: The oil layer is what stopped this nail from rusting
options.rationale: The oil is seen as a barrier coating rather than as the means of keeping air out of the water.

options.text: Boiling the water made the rusting reaction much slower
options.rationale: Rusting is treated as still happening, just slowed, because water is believed to be the only requirement.

mcqs.stem: In the rusting experiment, why is anhydrous calcium chloride sealed in the tube with one of the nails?

options.text: It absorbs the air, so only water can reach the nail
options.rationale: Students know the chemical removes something but attach it to the wrong variable.

options.text: It coats the nail in a barrier that keeps out damp
options.rationale: The added chemical is assumed to protect the metal directly, as grease or paint would.

options.text: It speeds up rusting, so a result is seen sooner
options.rationale: Added chemicals are assumed to be there to make the reaction work, not to remove a condition.

options.text: It absorbs water vapour, so the nail is left in dry air
options.rationale: Removing water while leaving air present is the control that tests whether water is necessary for rusting.

mcqs.stem: Greasing, painting and electroplating all prevent corrosion. How do they work?

options.text: They make the metal underneath much less reactive
options.rationale: Students look for a chemical change in the metal rather than simple physical separation.

options.text: They replace an oxide layer that has flaked off the metal
options.rationale: Oxide layers are assumed always to crumble, so a coating is seen as a replacement for one.

options.text: They form a barrier that keeps air and water off the metal
options.rationale: All three are barrier coatings: they separate the metal surface from the substances that would attack it.

options.text: They react with the metal to form a harder new compound
options.rationale: A chemical reaction sounds like a stronger explanation than a physical barrier.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?

options.text: Aluminium is unreactive, so air and water do not attack it
options.rationale: Observation contradicts the reactivity series, and students resolve it by deciding aluminium is unreactive.

options.text: Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh metal that is tougher
options.rationale: Rust is taken as the model for how every metal oxide behaves.

options.text: An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
options.rationale: Aluminium has an oxide coating that stays attached and protects the metal from further corrosion.

options.text: Aluminium is always painted before it is used outdoors
options.rationale: A barrier coating is the only protection mechanism the student has to hand.

mcqs.stem: Iron is galvanised by coating it with which metal?

options.text: Zinc
options.rationale: Zinc is used to galvanise iron; it is more reactive than iron and so protects it sacrificially.

options.text: Tin
options.rationale: Tin-plated cans are the other coated-iron example students meet, and any coating is assumed to work the same way.

options.text: Chromium
options.rationale: Chromium is associated with stainless, rust-free steel, so it is picked as the protective metal.

options.text: Copper
options.rationale: Copper is the familiar corrosion-resistant metal, so it is assumed to protect iron too.

mcqs.stem: Why does a zinc coating go on protecting iron even after the coating has been scratched through?

options.text: Zinc is less reactive, so air and water do not attack it
options.rationale: The rule that unreactive metals survive is transferred to the protecting metal.

options.text: The scratch seals itself as the soft zinc spreads into it
options.rationale: The coating is thought of only as a barrier, so protection must mean the gap being closed.

options.text: The zinc makes the iron beneath it less reactive than before
options.rationale: The coating is assumed to change the metal it covers rather than to corrode in its place.

options.text: Zinc is more reactive, so the zinc corrodes instead of iron
options.rationale: Sacrificial protection: the more reactive metal is attacked in preference, so exposed iron is still protected.

mcqs.stem: Blocks of magnesium are bolted to the steel hull of a ship. Why does this protect the steel?

options.text: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first
options.rationale: Sacrificial protection explained by relative reactivity: the more reactive magnesium is attacked instead of the iron.

options.text: Magnesium is less reactive than iron, so it resists the sea
options.rationale: Students expect the protecting metal to be the one that survives, so they invert the reactivity order.

options.text: Any metal bolted to a hull will corrode before the steel does
options.rationale: The zinc example is generalised without checking where the metal sits in the reactivity series.

options.text: The blocks spread out and seal the hull against the seawater
options.rationale: Protection is imagined only as a barrier, so the blocks are read as patching the surface.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the metals in everyday use is correct?

options.text: Most are compounds, formed when metals react together
options.rationale: Different properties from the parent metals are read as evidence that a new compound has formed.

options.text: Most are pure metals, refined to remove everything else
options.rationale: Purer is assumed to mean better, so useful metals are assumed to be pure ones.

options.text: Most are pure metals with a thin coat of a second metal
options.rationale: Plating has just been met as a way of improving a metal, so it is assumed to be the usual arrangement.

options.text: Most are alloys, which are mixtures containing a metal
options.rationale: Most metals in everyday use are alloys, and an alloy is a mixture rather than a compound.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about bronze and brass is correct?

options.text: Bronze is copper with zinc; brass is copper with tin
options.rationale: The two alloys are learnt together and share copper, so the second element is easily swapped.

options.text: Both are compounds made when copper reacts with a metal
options.rationale: Properties unlike those of copper are read as evidence that a new compound has formed.

options.text: Both are pure copper that has been hardened by heating
options.rationale: A named metal with better properties is assumed to be a treated pure metal, not a mixture.

options.text: Bronze is copper with tin; brass is copper with zinc
options.rationale: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

mcqs.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which use is it best matched to?

options.text: Statues and bells, which are cast from copper and tin
options.rationale: The classic bronze use is offered, and students who have swapped the two alloys take it.

options.text: Musical instruments such as trumpets, and taps and fittings
options.rationale: Brass is the alloy used for brass instruments and for taps, door fittings and similar fixtures.

options.text: Cutting blades and tools, which must be hard and brittle
options.rationale: The use belongs to high carbon steel, but any hard-sounding alloy is thought suitable for tools.

options.text: Aircraft panels, which need the lowest possible density
options.rationale: The aircraft use is memorable and gets attached to whichever alloy is being asked about.

mcqs.stem: A gold ring is sold as 18 carat. What does that tell you?

options.text: It is 18% gold, the rest being silver and copper
options.rationale: The carat number is read as a percentage, because percentages are the familiar proportional scale.

options.text: It has a mass of 18 carats, a unit used for gold
options.rationale: Carat is also a unit of mass for gemstones, so it is taken as a measure of how heavy the ring is.

options.text: It is 75% gold, alloyed with silver, copper and zinc
options.rationale: The carat scale runs to 24 for pure gold, and the specification gives 18 carat as 75% gold.

options.text: It is gold that has been mixed with 18 other metals
options.rationale: The number is read as a count of ingredients rather than as a proportion out of 24.

mcqs.stem: A bracelet is 12 carat gold. What percentage of it is gold?

options.rationale: 24 carat is 100% gold, so 12 carat is 12 out of 24, which is 50%.
The carat figure is copied straight across as a percentage.
The 24 of the scale is treated as a quantity in its own right rather than as the top of a proportion scale.
The one worked value in the specification, 18 carat = 75%, is recalled without redoing the proportion.

mcqs.stem: How do high carbon steel and low carbon steel differ?

options.text: High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon is softer
options.rationale: The specification states high carbon steel is strong but brittle, and low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped.

options.text: High carbon steel is stronger in every way and will not break
options.rationale: Strong is read as good on every measure, so brittleness is not registered as a cost.

options.text: High carbon steel is pure iron; low carbon steel is an alloy
options.rationale: Steel is thought of as purified iron, so less carbon is read as less pure.

options.text: Low carbon steel resists corrosion; high carbon steel does not
options.rationale: Corrosion resistance is the property of stainless steel and gets attached to the wrong steel.

mcqs.stem: Stainless steels are hard and resistant to corrosion. What are they?

options.text: Iron that has been electroplated with a layer of chromium
options.rationale: Stainless steel looks like chrome plating, and plating has just been met as a barrier coating.

options.text: A pure form of iron from which the carbon has been removed
options.rationale: Resistance to corrosion is credited to purity rather than to the alloying metals.

options.text: Iron alloyed with tin, a metal that does not corrode in damp
options.rationale: Tin plating on cans is remembered as a corrosion cure and transferred to the alloy.

options.text: Iron alloyed with chromium and nickel as well as carbon
options.rationale: Steels containing chromium and nickel are the stainless steels; the added metals are alloyed throughout.

mcqs.stem: Car body panels are pressed into shape from flat sheet. Which steel is used, and why?

options.text: Low carbon steel, because it is softer and easily shaped
options.rationale: Pressing sheet into shape needs a steel that can be deformed without cracking, which is low carbon steel.

options.text: Stainless steel, because a chromium plating can never rust
options.rationale: Rusting cars are a familiar problem, and stainless steel is seen as plated rather than alloyed.

options.text: High carbon steel, because it is much the strongest of them
options.rationale: The strongest material is assumed to be the right choice regardless of the job.

options.text: High carbon steel, because brittle metals bend most easily
options.rationale: Brittle is confused with soft, so brittleness is read as an advantage when shaping.

mcqs.stem: Why are aluminium alloys, rather than steels, used for aircraft bodies?

options.text: Aluminium alloys are low density, so the aircraft is lighter
options.rationale: Aluminium alloys are low density, which is the property that matters when mass must be lifted.

options.text: Aluminium is the strongest of all the metals used in industry
options.rationale: A demanding application is assumed to call for the strongest possible material.

options.text: Aluminium is unreactive, so the body will never need a coating
options.rationale: Aluminium's resistance to corrosion is credited to low reactivity rather than to its oxide layer.

options.text: Aluminium alloys melt at a higher temperature than all steels
options.rationale: An extreme use is assumed to demand an extreme property, and melting point is the one reached for.

mcqs.stem: A table gives two alloys. P: density 8.9 g/cm3, very hard, corrodes in damp air. Q: density 2.7 g/cm3, moderate strength, resists corrosion. Which is the better choice for a bicycle frame kept outdoors, and why?

options.text: P, because the hardest alloy always makes the best frame
options.rationale: A single ranking of materials from best to worst replaces matching a property to the job.

options.text: Q, because it is far less dense and it resists corrosion
options.rationale: A frame must be light and must survive outdoors, and the data show Q is better on both counts.

options.text: P, because a denser alloy is always the stronger of the two
options.rationale: Density is read as a measure of strength, so the heavier alloy looks like the tougher one.

options.text: Q, because low density is a sign of very high strength
options.rationale: The right alloy is picked for a reason the data do not support, which the strength column contradicts.

mcqs.stem: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?

options.text: Sand, boron trioxide and limestone
options.rationale: The two glass recipes are merged, with boron added to the everyday mixture.

options.text: Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
options.rationale: This is the mixture the specification gives for soda-lime glass.

options.text: Sand, sodium chloride and limestone
options.rationale: Soda in the name is taken as common salt rather than sodium carbonate.

options.text: Sodium carbonate and boron trioxide
options.rationale: Ingredients from both recipes are combined and the sand is dropped.

mcqs.stem: Why is borosilicate glass, rather than soda-lime glass, used for laboratory glassware that is heated?

options.text: It contains limestone, which stops the glass from melting
options.rationale: Limestone belongs to the soda-lime recipe and is credited with the heat resistance.

options.text: It melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass does
options.rationale: The specification states that borosilicate glass melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

options.text: It is a composite, so its fibres hold the shape when hot
options.rationale: Any material with useful properties is assumed to be a composite of two materials.

options.text: It is made from sand alone, so it has no impurities in it
options.rationale: Heat resistance is credited to purity, and the boron trioxide is forgotten.

mcqs.stem: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?

options.text: Clay is melted and then poured into a cold metal mould
options.rationale: Glass and metal shaping both involve melting, and the method is generalised to clay.

options.text: Dry clay powder is pressed hard, with no heating at all
options.rationale: Pressing is a familiar shaping method, and the firing step is forgotten.

options.text: Clay fibres are set into a matrix of cement or of resin
options.rationale: Composites are met in the same part of the topic and the structures are confused.

options.text: Wet clay is shaped, and then heated in a furnace
options.rationale: Clay ceramics are made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace.

mcqs.stem: Low density and high density poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. How can one monomer give two different materials?

options.text: The high density polymer is made from a heavier monomer
options.rationale: Students believe a different polymer must have come from a different monomer.

options.text: The high density polymer simply has much longer chains
options.rationale: Chain length is the only structural variable students have to hand.

options.text: The two are made using different catalysts and conditions
options.rationale: Properties of polymers depend on the monomers and on the conditions under which they are made, and here only the conditions differ.

options.text: One of them is a composite of ethene held in a matrix
options.rationale: Composite is used loosely for any material made in more than one way.

mcqs.stem: In terms of their structures, why do thermosetting polymers not melt when they are heated?

options.text: Their chains are far longer and heavier than in other plastics
options.rationale: The rule that longer molecules melt at higher temperatures is stretched to explain not melting at all.

options.text: The covalent bonds along their chains are much stronger ones
options.rationale: Melting is assumed to break bonds within the chains, so stronger bonds seem to be the answer.

options.text: Their chains are held to each other by covalent cross-links
options.rationale: Cross-links between the chains stop the chains moving apart, so the material cannot melt.

options.text: Their chains are packed more closely than in ordinary plastics
options.rationale: Close packing is borrowed from high density poly(ethene) and offered as a reason for not melting.

mcqs.stem: A plastic saucepan handle chars but does not soften when it is heated strongly. What does this show?

options.text: It is thermosetting, because such polymers do not melt
options.rationale: Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated, so charring without softening identifies one.

options.text: It is thermosoftening, but its chains are unusually long
options.rationale: Failure to melt is explained by chain length rather than by cross-linking.

options.text: It is thermosetting, but would melt if heated far hotter
options.rationale: Every substance is assumed to have a melting point, so not melting is read as melting later.

options.text: It is a clay ceramic, since these are fired in a furnace
options.rationale: Resistance to heat is associated with ceramics, and the material is reclassified.

mcqs.stem: Most composites are made of two materials. What are the two parts called?

options.text: Two metals melted together to give a single mixture
options.rationale: Composite is taken to mean any mixture of two materials, which describes an alloy.

options.text: A matrix or binder surrounding a reinforcement
options.rationale: A matrix or binder surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments of the reinforcement.

options.text: Fibres that surround and bind fragments of the matrix
options.rationale: Matrix suggests a framework, so the fibres and the binder get their labels swapped.

options.text: A coating on the outside and the material underneath
options.rationale: Barrier coatings were met earlier, and a two-part material is read as coated.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a composite material?

options.text: Concrete: fragments of gravel bound by cement
options.rationale: Cement is the matrix and the gravel fragments are the reinforcement, which fits the definition exactly.

options.text: Wool: natural fibres twisted together into yarn
options.rationale: Fibres are taken as the test for a composite, so anything fibrous qualifies.

options.text: Brass: copper and zinc melted to form a mixture
options.rationale: An alloy is a mixture of two materials, so it looks like a composite.

options.text: Pottery: wet clay shaped and fired in a furnace
options.rationale: Two named materials in this part of the topic are assumed to be related structures.

mcqs.stem: A table gives densities in g/cm3: steel 7.9, aluminium alloy 2.7, fibreglass 1.9, poly(ethene) 0.94. All of them are stiffer than poly(ethene). A part must be as light as possible but stiffer than a polymer. Which should be chosen?

options.text: Poly(ethene), because 0.94 g/cm3 is the lowest density listed
options.rationale: The density condition is used and the stiffness condition in the stem is ignored.

options.text: Steel, because at 7.9 g/cm3 the densest is always the stiffest
options.rationale: Density is treated as a measure of stiffness, so the heaviest material looks the most rigid.

options.text: Fibreglass, at 1.9 g/cm3 and stiffer than the polymer
options.rationale: Of the materials that meet the stiffness condition, fibreglass has the lowest density in the table.

options.text: Steel, because the strongest material given is the safest pick
options.rationale: Strength is used as an overall ranking, so the requirement to be light is set aside.

mcqs.stem: A saucepan handle must not melt, must not conduct heat well, and must be moulded cheaply in quantity. Which material is most appropriate?

options.text: A thermosoftening polymer, which softens only when charred
options.rationale: Thermosoftening polymers are assumed to hold out until they burn, so melting is not seen as a risk.

options.text: Stainless steel, the hardest and strongest of the choices
options.rationale: The strongest material is picked without checking it against the actual requirements.

options.text: A clay ceramic, melted and poured into the shape needed
options.rationale: Ceramics do resist heat, but the method described is wrong and shaping is not cheap this way.

options.text: A thermosetting polymer, which does not melt when heated
options.rationale: It meets every requirement: it does not melt, polymers are poor thermal conductors, and it can be moulded.
